```{r}
#| label: setup
#| echo: false
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(eco)
  library(data.table)
  library(lme4)
  library(ggplot2)
  library(plotly)
})
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))
options(digits = 3)
fmt <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, digits = d, format = "f")
# One fixed colour and shape per sampling protocol, in this order everywhere.
proto_levels <- c("camera_trap", "point_count", "line_transect", "acoustic")
proto_labels <- c("Camera trap", "Point count", "Line transect", "Acoustic recorder")
proto_cols <- setNames(c("#0072B2", "#E69F00", "#009E73", "#CC79A7"), proto_labels)
proto_shapes <- setNames(c(16, 17, 15, 18), proto_labels)
```

eco stores observations: a row for every survey of every unit, and a `y`. It
does not store what the species weighs, eats or how far it moves, because
that is not detection data and other people already maintain it well. Two
open trait databases cover the two classes most of the corpus is about,
AVONET for birds (Tobias et al. 2022) and COMBINE for mammals (Soria et al.
2021), both CC BY 4.0 and both keyed on the scientific names every eco
`__taxa` table carries. So the join happens here, when the page renders:
fetch the trait tables, match names, and ask a question that no single
deposit can answer on its own, whether a species' per-survey detection
probability scales with its body size.

::: {.callout-note}
This vignette, including the choice of tables, the analysis and the writing,
was produced largely by Claude (Anthropic) from a task specification, with
human review. Treat the interpretations accordingly; the code is all on the
page and runs from a clean session.
:::

## Why body mass

The usual expectation is that bigger animals are easier to detect: a larger
body is seen farther, a larger bird sings louder, a larger mammal triggers a
camera more reliably and from farther away. Distance sampling makes that
explicit by modelling detection as a function of distance and letting the
curve vary with species. Occupancy models do not; their $p$ is a single
per-survey probability that folds together how many individuals are at the
site, how far the survey reaches, and how conspicuous each one is. That last
part is where body mass should enter. The first two can pull the other way,
since larger species are typically rarer and range more widely, so fewer of
them are at any one site on any one visit. The corpus lets us see which
effect wins, and whether it depends on how the survey was done.

## Fetching the traits

`eco_traits()` downloads the two sources from figshare into the package cache
the first time it is called (AVONET's supplementary dataset is a 21 MB xlsx,
so it needs `readxl`), then reads them from disk. Nothing is written to eco.

```{r}
#| label: fetch
eco_set_version(3)
traits <- eco_traits()
setDT(traits)
traits[, .(species = .N, with_mass = sum(!is.na(body_mass_g)),
           median_mass_g = median(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)), by = .(source, taxon_group)]
```

```{r}
#| label: citations
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
cat(paste0("- ", attr(traits, "citations"), "\n"))
```

Body mass in AVONET is a species mean, mostly from Dunning's handbook, with
`body_mass_source` saying where each value came from. COMBINE's
`trait_data_reported.csv` is the reported layer, not the imputed one: a
species with no measured mass in the literature stays `NA` here rather than
being filled from relatives.

## Matching names

The join is by scientific name against each table's `__taxa`, with three
attempts per row: the exact `scientificName`, then GBIF's accepted name when
the deposit's name is a synonym, then the binomial when the deposit names a
subspecies. Codes above species rank (a genus, a family, "sp.") are never
matched. The tables are the bird and mammal site-level detection and count
tables for which the next section has a detection estimate.

```{r}
#| label: match
tags <- as.data.table(eco_tags())
corpus <- readRDS("traits_data/traits_corpus.rds")
fits <- corpus$fits
tables <- unique(fits$table)
joined <- rbindlist(lapply(tables, function(tb) {
  grp <- tags[table == tb]$taxon_group
  t <- as.data.table(eco_traits(eco_taxa(tb), group = tolower(grp)))
  t[, table := tb]
  t[, .(table, taxon, scientificName, taxonRank, body_mass_g, trait_match)]
}))
match_tab <- joined[, .(taxa = .N, matched = sum(trait_match != "none"),
                        with_mass = sum(!is.na(body_mass_g)),
                        exact = sum(trait_match == "exact"),
                        accepted = sum(trait_match == "accepted_name"),
                        binomial = sum(trait_match == "binomial")), by = table]
match_tab <- merge(match_tab, tags[, .(table, taxon_group, sampling_protocol)], by = "table")
setorder(match_tab, taxon_group, table)
knitr::kable(match_tab[, .(table, taxon_group, sampling_protocol, taxa, matched, with_mass, exact, accepted, binomial)],
             col.names = c("Table", "Group", "Protocol", "Taxa", "Matched", "With mass", "Exact", "Accepted name", "Binomial"))
```

Across the `r length(tables)` tables, `r sum(match_tab$matched)` of
`r sum(match_tab$taxa)` taxon codes match a trait row
(`r fmt(100 * sum(match_tab$matched) / sum(match_tab$taxa), 1)`%), and
`r sum(match_tab$with_mass)` carry a mass. The rest, and why:

```{r}
#| label: unmatched
unmatched <- joined[trait_match == "none" | is.na(body_mass_g)]
unmatched[, reason := fcase(
  trait_match != "none" & is.na(body_mass_g), "matched, no reported mass",
  !is.na(taxonRank) & taxonRank != "species", paste("rank:", taxonRank),
  scientificName %in% c("Felis catus"), "domestic form, not in COMBINE",
  scientificName %in% c("Varanus bengalensis"), "a reptile in a mammal table",
  default = "taxonomy edition (BirdLife v5 / IUCN 2020 vs GBIF backbone)")]
knitr::kable(unmatched[order(table, scientificName), .(table, taxon, scientificName, reason)],
             col.names = c("Table", "Code", "Name in __taxa", "Why"))
```

The taxonomy-edition misses are real species under another name: the pileated
woodpecker is *Hylatomus pileatus* in BirdLife's checklist, the willow tit
*Poecile montanus*, the fisher *Martes pennanti* in IUCN 2020. GBIF's accepted
name catches some synonyms but not splits and lumps that GBIF does not treat
as synonyms. A crosswalk through the BirdLife and IUCN name lists would close
most of these; for a first look at the question below, losing them changes
nothing.

## Detection from the corpus sweep

The detection probability is $\hat p$ from the null single-season occupancy
model $\psi(\cdot)\,p(\cdot)$ fitted to one species at a time, the same fit
the [occupancy vignette](occupancy.html) runs over the corpus. Twelve bird and
mammal tables come from that sweep's cache; the remaining tables were fitted
with the same recipe in
[`traits_compute.R`](https://github.com/ben-domingue/eco/blob/main/site/vignettes/traits_compute.R)
(counts collapsed to detection, multi-season tables reduced to their largest
primary period, a species never detected or surveyed once per site skipped).
Two tables that should be here are not: Snapshot USA
(`rooney_2025_snapshotusa_comm`, 87 mammals) is 800 MB, over the 100 MB cap
of the anonymous Redivis endpoint; the Banff snow-track table surveys most
segments once per winter, so $\psi$ and $p$ do not separate.

A boundary fit ($\hat\psi$ above 0.99 or $\hat p$ below 0.01) says the data
could not separate the two parameters, so those fits are dropped along with
non-converged ones. That removes many fits in the two-visit point-count
tables, where a species seen once at a few sites is consistent with being
everywhere and almost never detected.

```{r}
#| label: join
d <- merge(fits, joined[, .(table, taxon, scientificName, body_mass_g)], by = c("table", "taxon"))
d[, usable := converged & psi < 0.99 & p > 0.01 & !is.na(body_mass_g)]
d[, .(fits = .N, converged = sum(converged), boundary = sum(converged & !(psi < 0.99 & p > 0.01)),
      no_mass = sum(is.na(body_mass_g)), usable = sum(usable))]
d <- d[usable == TRUE]
d[, `:=`(logit_p = qlogis(p), log_mass = log10(body_mass_g))]
d[, protocol := factor(proto_labels[match(sampling_protocol, proto_levels)], levels = proto_labels)]
d[, log_mass_c := log_mass - mean(log_mass), by = table]
```

That leaves `r nrow(d)` species-by-table fits in `r uniqueN(d$table)` tables.
Hover a point for the species and table.

```{r}
#| label: scatter
#| fig-height: 5.5
d[, hover := sprintf("%s<br>%s<br>%s g, p = %s (%s)", scientificName, table,
                     format(round(body_mass_g), big.mark = ","), fmt(p), protocol)]
g <- ggplot(d, aes(log_mass, logit_p, colour = protocol, shape = protocol, text = hover)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = proto_cols, drop = FALSE) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = proto_shapes, drop = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:5, labels = c("1 g", "10 g", "100 g", "1 kg", "10 kg", "100 kg")) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = qlogis(c(0.02, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9)),
                     labels = c("0.02", "0.1", "0.3", "0.5", "0.7", "0.9")) +
  labs(x = "Body mass (log scale)", y = expression(hat(p) ~ "(logit scale)"), colour = NULL, shape = NULL)
ggplotly(g, tooltip = "text") |> layout(legend = list(orientation = "h", y = -0.2))
```

Pooled across tables there is no relation to speak of, and there should not
be: the tables differ in survey length, season, region and in what a
"survey" is, and the mammals, which are all camera trapped, are also all
heavier than the birds. The question is within a table. Each panel below is
one table with at least eight usable species, with an ordinary least-squares
line through its points.

```{r}
#| label: facets
#| fig-height: 8
big <- d[, if (.N >= 8) .SD, by = table]
big[, panel := sub("_(comm|count|nmix|dynocc)$", "", table)]
ggplot(big, aes(log_mass, logit_p, colour = protocol, shape = protocol)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = TRUE, linewidth = 0.7, fill = "grey80", colour = "grey30") +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free_x", ncol = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = proto_cols, drop = FALSE) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = proto_shapes, drop = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:5, labels = c("1 g", "10 g", "100 g", "1 kg", "10 kg", "100 kg")) +
  labs(x = "Body mass (log scale)", y = expression(hat(p) ~ "(logit scale)"), colour = NULL, shape = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", strip.text = element_text(size = 9))
```

## One model

Per-table slopes first, since they are what the panels show. The slope is the
change in logit $p$ per tenfold increase in body mass, with its standard
error from the least-squares fit, which ignores the uncertainty in each
$\hat p$ and so understates it.

```{r}
#| label: slopes
slopes <- big[, {
  m <- lm(logit_p ~ log_mass)
  .(n = .N, slope = coef(m)[[2]], se = summary(m)$coefficients[2, 2],
    protocol = protocol[1], taxon_group = taxon_group[1])
}, by = table]
setorder(slopes, slope)
slopes[, table := factor(table, levels = table)]
ggplot(slopes, aes(slope, table, colour = protocol, shape = protocol)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = slope - 1.96 * se, xmax = slope + 1.96 * se), height = 0, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = proto_cols, drop = FALSE) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = proto_shapes, drop = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Slope of logit p on log10 body mass (95% interval)", y = NULL, colour = NULL, shape = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#| label: slopes-table
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(slopes[, .(table, protocol, n, slope = fmt(slope), se = fmt(se))],
             col.names = c("Table", "Protocol", "Species", "Slope", "SE"))
```

Then one pooled model, logit $\hat p$ on log mass centred within table, with
a random intercept per table and an independent random slope. Centring makes
the fixed slope the average within-table slope and leaves the between-table
differences in mass to the intercepts.

```{r}
#| label: lmer
m1 <- lmer(logit_p ~ log_mass_c + (1 | table) + (0 + log_mass_c | table), data = d, REML = FALSE)
m0 <- lmer(logit_p ~ 1 + (1 | table) + (0 + log_mass_c | table), data = d, REML = FALSE)
cf <- summary(m1)$coefficients
vc <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(m1))
lrt <- anova(m0, m1)
print(cf)
```

```{r}
#| label: lmer-report
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
cat(sprintf(paste0(
  "The average within-table slope is %s (SE %s), on the logit scale per tenfold ",
  "increase in mass: a species ten times heavier than its table-mates is detected ",
  "with odds about %s%% %s per survey. The slope standard deviation across tables is %s, ",
  "so tables disagree about as much as the average says. The likelihood-ratio test ",
  "against the model with no fixed slope gives $\\chi^2$ = %s on 1 df, $p$ = %s. ",
  "The residual standard deviation is %s on the logit scale, which is to say that body ",
  "mass explains very little of why one species is detected more than another in the ",
  "same table.\n"),
  fmt(cf[2, 1]), fmt(cf[2, 2]),
  fmt(100 * abs(exp(cf[2, 1]) - 1), 0), if (cf[2, 1] < 0) "lower" else "higher",
  fmt(vc[vc$grp == "table.1", "sdcor"]), fmt(lrt$Chisq[2]), fmt(lrt$`Pr(>Chisq)`[2], 3),
  fmt(vc[vc$grp == "Residual", "sdcor"])))
```

So the average slope points the other way from the "bigger is easier"
expectation, and most tables agree on the sign, but the pooled test does not
reject zero and no single table's slope is more than about two standard
errors from it. The Swiss breeding bird survey, with its long line transects
and territory mapping, is the one large table where the slope is positive.
Read with the caveat from the top: an occupancy $p$ is a per-survey, per-site probability, and larger
species are at fewer sites in smaller numbers, so a lower $\hat p$ for a
larger species need not mean each individual is harder to detect. Separating
the two needs abundance, which the count tables here have and this null fit
throws away. That is the next vignette, not this one.

## Where this goes

Three things are visible from this page that a single deposit cannot show.
The name match is good enough to use (`r fmt(100 * sum(match_tab$matched) / sum(match_tab$taxa), 0)`% of codes) but the misses are
systematic, from taxonomy editions, and a crosswalk through the BirdLife and
IUCN name lists would be a small, reusable fix. Nothing about the join needed
anything stored: `eco_traits()` is forty lines over two downloads, and a third
source for amphibians, fish or reptiles would be another twenty. And the
question itself is better posed with abundance than with occupancy, which the
same tables support.

## Reproducibility

Source: [`site/vignettes/traits.qmd`](https://github.com/ben-domingue/eco/blob/main/site/vignettes/traits.qmd)
and [`traits_compute.R`](https://github.com/ben-domingue/eco/blob/main/site/vignettes/traits_compute.R)
in the eco repository. The null-model fits were run on `r corpus$date_run`
(the twelve tables shared with the occupancy sweep on
`r corpus$occupancy_sweep_date`). Data were read with `eco_set_version(3)`,
so a later release of the warehouse does not change the page. The trait
tables are fetched when the page renders from the pinned figshare versions
below; a newer version of either database would change the page only if the
downloaded file ids were changed in the package.

```{r}
#| label: versions
#| echo: false
v <- eco_version()
cat(sprintf("eco version %s (Redivis eco %s, eco_meta %s, released %s)\n",
            v$eco_version, v$eco, v$eco_meta, substr(v$released, 1, 10)))
cat(paste0(unique(traits$source), ": ", unique(traits$source_version), "\n"), sep = "")
cat(sprintf("R %s; eco %s; unmarked %s; lme4 %s; readxl %s\n",
            getRversion(), packageVersion("eco"), packageVersion("unmarked"),
            packageVersion("lme4"), packageVersion("readxl")))
```

References. Tobias, J. A., Sheard, C., Pigot, A. L., et al. (2022). AVONET:
morphological, ecological and geographical data for all birds. *Ecology
Letters* 25, 581–597. Soria, C. D., Pacifici, M., Di Marco, M., Stephen, S.
M. and Rondinini, C. (2021). COMBINE: a coalesced mammal database of
intrinsic and extrinsic traits. *Ecology* 102, e03344. MacKenzie, D. I.,
Nichols, J. D., Lachman, G. B., Droege, S., Royle, J. A. and Langtimm, C. A.
(2002). Estimating site occupancy rates when detection probabilities are less
than one. *Ecology* 83, 2248–2255. Bates, D., Mächler, M., Bolker, B. and
Walker, S. (2015). Fitting linear mixed-effects models using lme4. *Journal of
Statistical Software* 67(1).
